name: Articles
summary: Choosing a, an, the or no article.

paragraphs: Articles are the small words a, an and the. They appear in almost every sentence in English, yet they cause problems for learners at every level. If your first language does not use separate words like a and the, articles can feel unnecessary, and it is easy to leave them out or put them in the wrong place.

The good news is that articles are not random. Each choice answers one simple question for the reader: are you talking about any one thing, a specific thing the reader can identify, or things in general? Once you learn to ask that question, most article decisions become logical.

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.text: Any one → a / an. A specific one → the. Things in general → no article.

rows: you mean one thing, but not a specific one
the reader knows exactly which one
The laptop on my desk is new.
you mean things in general (plural or uncountable)

paragraphs: Article errors are among the most frequent mistakes in IELTS writing, and because articles appear so often, the errors add up quickly. Examiners do not expect perfection, but frequent missing or wrong articles make your writing look less accurate and can affect your Grammatical Range and Accuracy score.
Articles also matter in Task 1, where phrases such as the number of, the highest and by the end of the period appear in almost every report.

Before you choose an article, you need to know what kind of noun you are using. Countable nouns can be counted (one book, two books). Uncountable nouns cannot (information, traffic, advice) and have no plural form.
This one detail decides which articles are even possible, as the table below shows.

sections.title: Rule 1: A singular countable noun never stands alone
sections.label: Rule 1: A singular countable noun never stands alone

paragraphs: This is the most important article rule, and the one broken most often in IELTS essays. A singular countable noun, such as problem, solution or city, cannot appear on its own. It always needs something in front of it: a, an, the, or another word such as this, my, every or one.
If you remember only one thing from this page, remember this: whenever you write a singular countable noun, check what comes before it.

items.text: Pollution is serious problem.
Pollution is a serious problem.
This is effective solution.
This is an effective solution.

sections.title: Rule 2: A or an? Listen to the first sound
sections.label: Rule 2: A or an? Listen to the first sound

paragraphs: Many learners choose between a and an by looking at the first letter of the next word. The real rule is about sound, not spelling. Use an before a vowel sound and a before a consonant sound.

Most of the time, the letter and the sound match. The tricky cases are words that start with a vowel letter but a consonant sound (university sounds like “you-niversity”), or with a consonant letter but a vowel sound (hour, where the h is silent).

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: The article depends on the word right after it, which may be an adjective rather than the noun: a reliable system, an essential part.

sections.title: Rule 3: First mention a, second mention the
sections.label: Rule 3: First mention a, second mention the

paragraphs: When you introduce something for the first time, the reader does not yet know which one you mean, so you use a or an. Once you have mentioned it, the reader knows exactly which one you are talking about, so from then on you use the.
You already do this naturally in everyday stories: “I saw a dog in the park. The dog was chasing a ball.” The same pattern works in essays and Task 1 reports.

items.text: The city built a new bridge in 2010. The bridge reduced traffic in the center.
The glass is melted in a furnace. The furnace heats it to a very high temperature.

sections.title: Rule 4: Use the when the reader knows which one
sections.label: Rule 4: Use the when the reader knows which one

paragraphs: The is used when the reader can identify exactly which thing you mean. Sometimes this is because you mentioned it before (Rule 3), but often it is because the rest of the phrase makes it specific. A phrase beginning with of very often does this.
Compare the cost (which cost? not clear) with the cost of living (now we know exactly which cost). The of-phrase points to one particular thing, so the is needed.

items.text: The cost of living has risen sharply.
The quality of education in rural areas is improving.
Smoking increases a risk of heart disease.
Smoking increases the risk of heart disease.

sections.title: Rule 5: Superlatives, ordinals and “only” words take the
sections.label: Rule 5: Superlatives, ordinals and “only” words take the

paragraphs: When something is the highest, the first or the only one, there can be just one of it, so the reader always knows which one you mean. That is why superlatives (the biggest, the most popular), ordinal numbers (the first, the second, the last) and words like only, same and main take the.
This rule appears constantly in Task 1, where you compare figures and describe the stages of a process.

rows: the highest rate, the most popular choice, the least expensive option
the first stage, the second year, the last decade
the only option, the same period, the main reason

items.text: Food accounted for largest share of spending.
Food accounted for the largest share of spending.

sections.title: Rule 6: Things there is only one of
sections.label: Rule 6: Things there is only one of

paragraphs: Some things are unique in our world or in our shared experience. There is only one internet, one sun and one environment that we all live in. Because the reader always knows which one you mean, these nouns take the.
The same logic applies to institutions that people usually think of as one: the government (of a country), the police, the public.

rows: the internet, the sun, the world, the environment
the government, the police, the public

items.text: Many students lack access to internet.
Many students lack access to the internet.

sections.title: Rule 7: No article for things in general
sections.label: Rule 7: No article for things in general

paragraphs: When you talk about things in general, meaning all of them as a category, use a plural or uncountable noun with no article. This is one of the most common places where learners add an unnecessary the.
Ask yourself: do I mean specific people or things, or that type of thing in general? If you mean the whole category, leave the article out.

rows: The children in this school need more sleep.
The pollution in this city is getting worse.
The technology used in hospitals is expensive.

items.text: The young people spend hours on social media.
Young people spend hours on social media.
We must protect the nature.
We must protect nature.

sections.title: Rule 8: Names of countries, cities and languages
sections.label: Rule 8: Names of countries, cities and languages

paragraphs: Most names of people, cities, countries, continents and languages take no article: Bangladesh, Dhaka, Asia, English. The main exceptions are countries whose names include a word such as states, kingdom or republic, or whose names are plural.
These exceptions are worth memorizing, because they appear often in Task 1 reports that compare countries.

rows: the UK, the USA, the United Arab Emirates
the Pacific, the Amazon (oceans and rivers)

sections.title: Rule 9: Learn fixed expressions as chunks
sections.label: Rule 9: Learn fixed expressions as chunks

paragraphs: Some common expressions follow their own pattern, and the easiest way to handle them is to learn them as complete chunks. Many describe everyday places and routines, where we use no article when we mean the activity rather than the building.
For example, go to school means going there to study. Go to the school suggests visiting the building for another reason, such as a parents’ meeting.
Task 1 reports use a small set of phrases again and again, and most of them contain articles. Learning these as fixed patterns saves time and removes a whole group of errors from your reports.
Notice that changes (a rise, a fall) usually take a, because you are describing one change among many possible ones, while specific measurements (the number, the highest point) take the.

rows: the number of / the proportion of
by the end of the period
By the end of the period, sales had doubled.
over the period / in the first year
Over the period, prices rose steadily.
a sharp rise / a slight fall
There was a sharp rise in 2015.
The rest was spent on transport.

blocks.title: The + adjective for groups of people
paragraphs: In Task 2, you may want to talk about a whole group of people described by an adjective. In this case, use the + adjective with a plural verb: the elderly, the poor, the unemployed, the young.

items.text: The elderly need better healthcare.
Governments should do more to support the unemployed.

paragraphs: Here is how these rules appear in real IELTS writing. Notice how Task 1 depends on the and Task 2 depends on knowing when to leave the article out.

rows: The number of international students rose sharply.
Food accounted for the largest share.
There was a slight fall in 2015.
Pollution is a serious problem in many cities.
Many people still lack access to the internet.
Children should learn a second language at an early age.

paragraphs: These five errors are among the most common in IELTS essays. Checking for them alone will remove most article mistakes from your writing.

rows: Coal had the highest share in 2010.

paragraphs: Use this quick routine during your final check. It works noun by noun.

steps: Find each noun in the sentence.
Singular and countable? It needs a, an, the or another word in front. It can never stand alone.
Does the reader know exactly which one? Use the.
Plural or uncountable, and meant in general? Use no article.

cards.front: I bought ____ umbrella yesterday because it was raining.
cards.why: Umbrella begins with a vowel sound (“um”), so we use an.

cards.front: My cousin is studying at ____ university in Canada.
cards.why: University begins with a vowel letter but a consonant sound (“you”), so we use a. The sound decides, not the spelling.

cards.front: Air pollution is ____ serious problem in many cities.
cards.why: Problem is a singular countable noun, so it cannot stand alone. It is any one problem, not a specific one, so we use a.

cards.front: I read an article about climate change. ____ article said that temperatures are rising fast.
cards.why: The article was already mentioned in the first sentence, so the reader knows exactly which one. Second mention takes the.

cards.front: Mount Everest is ____ highest mountain in the world.
cards.why: Highest is a superlative. There can be only one highest mountain, so we use the.

cards.front: Most young people spend hours on ____ internet every day.
cards.why: There is only one internet, so the reader always knows which one you mean.

cards.front: ____ children need plenty of sleep to grow properly.
cards.why: This is about children in general, not a specific group, so no article is needed. Compare: The children in my class are tired.

cards.front: ____ cost of living in big cities has risen sharply.
cards.why: The phrase “of living” tells us exactly which cost, so the noun is specific and takes the.

cards.front: In 2015, there was ____ sharp rise in house prices.
cards.why: A rise is one change being introduced for the first time, so we use a. Task 1 pattern: a sharp rise, a slight fall.

cards.front: She plans to study in ____ United Kingdom next year.
cards.why: Most country names take no article, but names with words like kingdom, states or republic take the: the UK, the USA.
